summary: Kyle Corbitt, co-founder and CEO of OpenPipe, delivers a talk on the GenAI maturity curve, addressing when organizations should consider fine-tuning LLMs. Despite his company being a fine-tuning platform, he candidly states that most audience members probably do not need fine-tuning yet. The presentation is organized into three sections: why, when, and how to fine-tune. The 'why' section introduces the Pareto Frontier concept, plotting output quality against tokens per dollar. Larger models generally produce higher quality but cost more. Inference-time techniques like Mixture of Agents can push beyond this frontier but at high cost and latency. Fine-tuning moves the entire Pareto Frontier outward, as demonstrated with real customer evaluations across four datasets using LLM-as-judge, where fine-tuned Llama 3 70B and 8B outperformed all baseline prompted models. Trade-offs include upfront time investment and reduced model flexibility on out-of-domain tasks. The 'when' section identifies three triggers: cost (when large model unit economics are unsustainable), latency (smaller fine-tuned models need fewer computations), and quality consistency (when a model succeeds 80-90% of the time but fails on format or instructions). Corbitt recommends starting with a prompted model like GPT-4 to benefit from iteration speed, then fine-tuning once the product shape is defined. The 'how' section covers four steps: prepare data, train, evaluate, and deploy. Starting with a prompted model in production lets you capture the actual input distribution by logging prompts, solving the classic ML challenge of knowing what your data looks like. Data preparation involves logging production prompts and optionally relabeling with human review or stronger models via iterative Mixture of Agents. Training is described as a largely solved problem with one-click tools. Evaluation splits into inner loop (fast LLM-as-judge) and outer loop (business-specific production metrics via AB testing). Deployment options include self-hosting with vLLM or TGI, or hosted inference providers. Corbitt notes engineers with no ML background have achieved successful fine-tuned models in under an hour, and fine-tuned models can deliver better performance than GPT-4 at 1/25th the cost.

sections.title: Introduction and Talk Structure
sections.summary: Kyle Corbitt introduces himself as CEO of OpenPipe, a fine-tuning platform. He acknowledges the awkward title 'You Probably Don't Need Fine Tuning' and states most audience members likely don't need fine-tuning yet. The talk is structured into three parts: why, when, and how to fine-tune.

sections.title: Why Fine-Tune: The Pareto Frontier
sections.summary: Introduces the Pareto Frontier plotting quality vs. tokens per dollar. Larger models are generally better but more expensive. Mixture of Agents can push beyond the frontier but at high cost. Fine-tuning moves the entire frontier outward, as demonstrated with real customer evaluations: fine-tuned Llama 3 70B and 8B outperformed all baseline prompted models across four datasets using LLM-as-judge.

sections.title: Trade-offs of Fine-Tuning
sections.summary: Despite the Pareto Frontier expansion, fine-tuning has trade-offs: the upfront time cost of gathering data and training, and reduced flexibility since tuned models specialize in one task and degrade on out-of-domain inputs. Clear task understanding is essential before fine-tuning.

sections.title: When to Fine-Tune: Three Triggers
sections.summary: Introduces three triggers for moving from prompted to fine-tuned models: cost (when large model unit economics are unsustainable), latency (smaller fine-tuned models need fewer computations), and quality consistency (when a model succeeds 80-90% of the time but fails on format or instructions the remaining 10-20%). Corbitt recommends starting with a prompted model to benefit from iteration speed, then fine-tuning once the product shape is defined.

sections.title: How to Fine-Tune: Four-Step Workflow
sections.summary: Covers the four-step fine-tuning process: prepare data, train, evaluate, and deploy. Data preparation starts by logging production prompts from a prompted model to capture the real input distribution. If the base model makes mistakes, human review or relabeling with a stronger model via iterative Mixture of Agents may be needed. Training is described as a largely solved problem with one-click tools like OpenPipe and open-source libraries. Evaluation splits into inner loop (fast LLM-as-judge for quick feedback) and outer loop (business-specific production metrics via AB testing). Deployment options include self-hosting with vLLM or TGI, or hosted inference providers. Engineers with no ML background have succeeded in under an hour. Fine-tuned models can achieve better performance than GPT-4 at 1/25th the cost.
